body:
Gujarat under colonial rule

During British rule, the territory of present-day Gujarat did not form a single administrative province. Some districts were governed directly by the British as part of the Bombay Presidency, while numerous princely states retained their rulers under British political supremacy.

Direct British rule meant that colonial officials administered revenue, policing and other government functions. In princely states, local rulers continued to exercise varying degrees of internal authority, but British residents or political agents supervised important political matters. Consequently, land revenue, local taxes, public works and relations with forest communities could differ considerably between neighbouring territories.

Three connected economic regions

Gujarat's colonial economy can be understood through three broad, connected regions.

  • Coastal and trading centres: Surat, Bharuch, Khambhat and Bhavnagar connected merchants, craftspeople and agricultural producers with maritime markets. Their commercial importance changed as colonial trade increasingly concentrated in ports controlled by the British.
  • Agricultural and manufacturing centres: Ahmedabad and the cotton-growing districts of central and western Gujarat supplied textiles, agricultural produce, merchants and labour. During the 19th century, factory production became increasingly important in Ahmedabad.
  • Eastern hills and forests: Panchmahals, Jambughoda, Chhota Udepur, Rajpipla and adjoining areas supported communities whose livelihoods combined cultivation, forest produce, grazing and other activities. Changes in political control and revenue demands contributed to resistance.

These were not isolated economies. Cotton grown in villages could pass through inland merchants to a railway station or port. Textiles produced in towns reached distant markets. Forest produce moved through local traders to commercial centres. Changes in the price of cotton, access to transport or control over land could therefore affect several groups differently.

Why political differences matter

Ahmedabad's industrial development and resistance in the Jambughoda region occurred under different immediate administrative arrangements. Ahmedabad's growth involved trade, mills and transport within the wider colonial economy. In the eastern belt, British officials, princely rulers and local chiefs could all make competing claims over authority and revenue.

Colonial influence did not always mean direct British administration. A princely state could retain its ruler while British intervention still affected its political decisions, finances and treatment of local communities.

Prelims focus

  • The Bombay Presidency included directly administered areas of Gujarat.
  • Baroda, Bhavnagar, Rajpipla and Chhota Udepur were among Gujarat's princely states.
  • Surat was an important maritime trading centre; Ahmedabad subsequently became a major cotton-mill centre.
  • Panchmahals and Jambughoda were important locations of Naikda resistance.
  • Trap: Present-day Gujarat must not be treated as one uniform British-administered province throughout the colonial period.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, ch. 6, Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners, pp. 65-74; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Rewa Kantha, ch. VII, pp. 61-66, 1880, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Bhavnagar District Administration, History of Bhavnagar, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Maritime trade connected Gujarat's coastal towns with inland producers and overseas markets.

title: Colonial Gujarat: Political Divisions and Economic Regions

body:
Surat's earlier commercial importance

In the 17th century, Surat was among the leading ports of Indian Ocean commerce. Indian merchants and foreign trading companies used it to exchange textiles and other goods with regions such as West Asia, East Africa and Europe. The English and Dutch trading companies were active at the port from the early 17th century.

Surat's importance depended on more than ships. Inland merchants arranged supplies from producers, brokers negotiated transactions, and bankers and money changers provided credit. Textile production in Gujarat was therefore connected with a wider commercial network.

Why Surat's trade declined

During the 18th century, Surat's earlier position weakened. Political instability, disruption of established commercial arrangements and the growing power of European trading companies affected the older merchant-controlled trading system. The English East India Company increasingly obtained commercial privileges and political authority.

At the same time, British-controlled ports, particularly Bombay, gained importance. Trade through such ports came to depend increasingly on European shipping, finance and commercial institutions. The shift of business towards Bombay reduced Surat's relative importance as a major international port.

A Class 10 history account gives a useful indication of the earlier contraction: the gross value of trade passing through Surat was approximately Rs 16 million in the closing years of the 17th century, compared with approximately Rs 3 million by the 1740s. These are historical trade-value estimates for the stated periods, not present-day prices.

Decline did not mean disappearance

Surat did not simply cease to be an economic centre. Merchants, bankers and artisans continued to operate there. Silk weaving, zari work and other specialised trades helped sustain the city's commercial life, although its earlier dominance in maritime trade was reduced.

It is important to distinguish decline in a city's relative importance from the complete disappearance of economic activity. A port could lose much of its international business while continuing as a regional centre of crafts, commerce and services.

Surat, Bombay and Ahmedabad performed different roles

Two developments must not be confused. Surat's earlier maritime position declined partly as colonial trade shifted towards Bombay. Separately, Ahmedabad developed into a major centre of mechanised cotton-textile production during the 19th century.

Surat to Bombay: a shift in the leading maritime trading network.
Ahmedabad's growth: the rise of an inland industrial centre based especially on cotton textiles.

Prelims focus

  • Surat was a leading Indian Ocean port in the 17th century.
  • English and Dutch trading vessels used Surat from the early 17th century.
  • Trade passing through Surat was estimated at about Rs 16 million in the late 17th century and Rs 3 million by the 1740s.
  • Bombay gained importance as colonial maritime trade expanded.
  • Surat retained specialised commercial and craft activities despite its relative decline.
  • Trap: Ahmedabad's rise as a textile city did not mean that it directly replaced Surat as an international seaport.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, ch. 6, Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners, p. 65; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, The Making of a Global World, section on the changing Indian trading network; Douglas E. Haynes, Rhetoric and Ritual in Colonial India, ch. 3, The Urban Economy, section Decline without Collapse, University of California Press, 1991, consulted online 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Surat’s trade fell from about Rs 16 million in the late 17th century to Rs 3 million by the 1740s, before Bombay’s later rise as a colonial port.
pictures.caption: Surat's recorded trade contraction preceded the major expansion of colonial port networks.

title: Surat: From a Major Indian Ocean Port to a Changed Trading Economy

body:
Gujarat's established textile traditions

Long before large cotton mills appeared, Gujarat was an important producer of woven, dyed and decorated textiles. Its craftspeople supplied local consumers as well as distant commercial markets.

  • Patola: a valued patterned silk textile associated historically with weaving centres including Surat, Ahmedabad and Patan. Patola cloth was also appreciated in Southeast Asian markets, particularly Indonesia.
  • Bandhani or bandanna: textiles produced by tying portions of cloth before dyeing them, thereby creating patterns. Gujarat and Rajasthan were important centres of this tie-and-dye tradition.
  • Zari and other decorated textiles: specialised textile crafts, including the use of decorative metallic thread, formed part of Gujarat's skilled production and helped sustain centres such as Surat.

Production required several kinds of skill. Spinners prepared yarn, weavers made cloth, dyers coloured it, and specialist craftspeople produced prints or decorative work. A decline in textile demand therefore affected not only individual weavers but an entire network of occupations.

How British industrialisation changed the market

Britain's industrialisation made it possible to produce cotton textiles in large quantities using machines. British manufacturers sought wider markets for these goods, including India.

Indian textiles faced two disadvantages. First, Indian producers encountered restrictions and duties in British markets. Second, machine-made British cloth increasingly entered Indian markets and competed with locally manufactured cloth. By the 1830s, imported British cotton textiles had become a major presence in India.

The change is often described as deindustrialisation: the decline or displacement of traditional manufacturing occupations without an equivalent immediate expansion of alternative industrial employment. It did not mean that every Indian craft disappeared. Certain handwoven fabrics retained customers because of their distinctive designs, methods and quality.

From exporting cloth to exporting cotton

Earlier, Indian merchants exported substantial quantities of finished textiles. Under colonial rule, Britain increasingly treated India as a source of agricultural raw materials and a market for manufactured products. Raw cotton could leave India for British factories, while machine-made cotton cloth returned for sale in Indian markets.

This was not a complete or permanent disappearance of Indian textile production. Ahmedabad's mills later developed alongside surviving handloom industries. Nevertheless, the growing connection between raw-cotton exports and imported manufactured cloth marked an important change in the structure of trade.

Effects on workers and households

When traditional weaving lost markets, some artisans had to seek employment in agriculture, migrate to towns or enter emerging factories. Rural spinning was also affected because imported yarn reduced demand for some kinds of hand-spun thread. The gains from expanding international trade were therefore not distributed equally among merchants, cultivators and artisans.

Prelims focus

  • Patola weaving was historically associated with Surat, Ahmedabad and Patan.
  • Bandhani is a tie-and-dye textile tradition associated with Gujarat and Rajasthan.
  • British machine-made cloth increasingly competed with Indian textiles during the 19th century.
  • Colonial trade encouraged exports of raw cotton and imports of manufactured cotton cloth.
  • Deindustrialisation refers to the weakening of traditional manufacturing activities.
  • Trap: The decline of handloom production did not mean that all Indian textile crafts disappeared.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, ch. 6, Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners, pp. 66-74; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 11, ch. 2, Colonial Rule and Crafts, pp. 15-23; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, ch. 1, Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence, pp. 4-8.]

pictures.alt: India supplied finished cotton and silk; expanding colonial trade sent raw cotton to Britain and cloth to India, while some specialised weaving continued.
pictures.caption: Colonial trade increasingly combined Indian raw-material exports with imports of British manufactured cloth.

title: Gujarat's Textiles and the Changing Pattern of Colonial Trade

body:
The emergence of factory production

Ahmedabad already had merchants, financial resources and established textile skills before modern mills appeared. Its transformation into an industrial city occurred when entrepreneurs invested in machinery, factory buildings and organised production.

Ranchhodlal Chhotalal was a pioneer of Ahmedabad's cotton-mill industry. The foundation of his textile venture dates to 1859, while Ahmedabad's first cotton mill began operating in 1861. These dates refer to different stages of the same development and should not be interchanged.

For comparison, the first cotton spinning mill in Bombay was established in 1854. Ahmedabad's industrial development therefore followed the emergence of modern cotton-mill production in Bombay.

Why Ahmedabad developed as a textile centre

Several conditions supported its growth:

  • Capital: Gujarati merchants and investors could mobilise funds for factory ventures.
  • Commercial experience: existing trading networks helped entrepreneurs obtain cotton, arrange credit and sell cloth.
  • Labour: workers could be recruited from the city and surrounding rural areas.
  • Transport: developing railway connections improved movement of cotton, machinery and finished products.

Not every condition was favourable at the beginning. Machinery had to be brought from abroad, transport was initially difficult, and Indian mills had to compete with imported British cloth. The establishment of a mill was therefore not the same as immediate industrial dominance.

The Bombay, Baroda and Central India Railway

The Bombay, Baroda and Central India Railway, generally abbreviated as BB&CI Railway, was incorporated in 1855. Its early construction included the section between Ankleshwar and Utran. The railway network developed through western India, and the line was extended to Bombay in 1864.

Rail transport improved connections among producing districts, inland commercial centres and ports. Cotton could be transported more efficiently to markets, while imported cloth and machinery could also move inland. Thus, the railway served both Indian manufacturing interests and the commercial requirements of the colonial economy.

Industrial growth and its limitations

Ahmedabad's cotton industry expanded during the later 19th century. The Ahmedabad Millowners Association was established in 1891. The city's concentration of textile mills eventually earned it the description Manchester of India.

The First World War, 1914-1918, created an important opportunity for Indian cotton mills. British textile imports were disrupted, and Indian factories received additional demand. This helped industrial expansion, although competition from imported goods remained a major challenge in the broader colonial period.

Prelims focus

  • Ranchhodlal Chhotalal pioneered Ahmedabad's cotton-mill industry.
  • The first Ahmedabad mill was founded as a venture in 1859 and commenced operation in 1861.
  • Bombay's first cotton spinning mill was established in 1854.
  • BB&CI Railway was incorporated in 1855; its network reached Bombay in 1864.
  • Ahmedabad Millowners Association was established in 1891.
  • Trap: The year 1859 refers to the foundation of Ahmedabad's first mill venture; 1861 is the standard year for the mill's commencement.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, ch. 6, Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners, pp. 73-74; Ahmedabad Textile Mills Association, A Brief History of the Textile Industry in Ahmedabad, section 1859-1980s, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of India, Western Railway, About Us, BB&CI Railway history, reviewed 10 September 2026, consulted 20 November 2026; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, The Age of Industrialisation, sections on factories in India and industrial growth.]

pictures.caption: Mechanised cotton mills brought factory production and wage labour into Ahmedabad's economy.
